title: The Optimist: Prelude and Fugue No.12, Book I
content_blocks: Eagerly, excitedly, trippingly, the music tumbles down from the top of the piano to the bottom, in groups of 2, 3, 4, and 6 notes—so enthusiastic is the music to bring itself to the listener that it practically “skips a beat.” These cascades of notes start overlapping, slowly at first and then more frequently; the amount of energy they bring to the bottom results in ricochets back toward the top, only to fall back again in a waterfall of notes. This leads, finally, to a rocking timpani-like boom-boom-boom in the bottom, settling on B, the first and last note and the tonic of this piece.

The enthusiasm of the prelude continues with the fugue: so eager is it that the first note of the fugue comes in early, overlapping with the end of the prelude. The early entrance of the first note continues throughout the fugue, turning what would otherwise have been a quite-ordinary fugue subject into an unusual one.

The fugue is also in the same unusual mode that we saw in Prelude and Fugue No.6 (see the July 2 post, and the July 3 explainer), which is more and more spread out as it gets closer to the very top and very bottom of the piano, and more compressed in the center. This means that the same melodic contour may feature large leaps at the extremes of the piano, or smaller leaps or steps in the center. In this center register a surprise happens: I found myself quoting a melody from Peter Warlock’s Pretty Ring Time (his setting of Shakespeare’s “It was a lover and a lass”) which becomes a new, second fugue subject—resulting in a double fugue (see Single, Double, and Triple Fugues, an Explainer, August 2, 2025).

The impatience of Fugue 12 continues into Prelude-and-Fugue 13: the very first note of the following piece overlaps the end of Fugue 12, uniting Numbers 12 and 13 into one. I’ll write about Number 13 in my next post. In the meantime, you can listen to David Kaplan’s enthusiastic performance of the eager Prelude and the impatient—“Optimistic”? (following the name I gave it four years ago)—Fugue, and you can also watch a video of Numbers 12 and 13 played without a break.
Impatient throughout, the music tumbles down from the top of the piano to the bottom, and then starts the fugue early.
